headline: High: RD-Agent’s broad networked API use can leak or misapply outputs, while awesome-prompts can be treated as trusted prompt content in shared workflows.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-prompts is a prompt/content-writing source, so its outputs can be copied into RD-Agent workflows and treated as instructions. RD-Agent has browser and API access, making instruction-following content more dangerous if pasted or ingested. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than observed.
conditions: IF awesome-prompts content is copied into RD-Agent prompts or task text
IF RD-Agent parses pasted prompt collections as authoritative instructions
mitigations: Review copied prompt text before use
Prefix imported content as data, not instructions
Use a separate staging workspace for prompt libraries
Disable browser/API actions during prompt import
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to imported prompt content

B_data_leakage.rationale: RD-Agent touches financial reports, logs, execution traces, and uses broad network egress plus external APIs, so sensitive material can leave the local environment. awesome-prompts itself shows no data-touching or egress, so the leakage risk is primarily from RD-Agent consuming or transmitting shared inputs. The pairwise path is plausible in default research workflows.
conditions: IF shared inputs include logs, reports, or datasets
IF RD-Agent sends those inputs to OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, DeepSeek, or Kaggle APIs
mitigations: Exclude secrets from shared inputs
Redact logs before handing them to RD-Agent
Use a separate workspace for prompt libraries and research data
Rotate any API keys used by RD-Agent
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention filters on outbound API calls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-prompts has no write surfaces or network egress, while RD-Agent has broad network/API access and multiple-instance support. There is no documented shared mutable resource or overlapping write target, so direct capability conflict is limited. Uncertainty is low because the profiles do not show a common writable surface.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same writable directory
IF an external orchestrator gives them shared mutable state
mitigations: Keep separate working directories
Run only one writer at a time
Mount prompt libraries read-only
Check for accidental shared log paths
requires-engineering: add file locking around shared outputs

D_cascading_error.rationale: awesome-prompts can supply prompt templates or instructions that RD-Agent may use in research and development tasks. RD-Agent’s browser/API automation means downstream actions can follow those prompts without strong verification. The pairwise pathway is plausible, but the profiles do not prove automatic trust, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF RD-Agent uses awesome-prompts text as a task template
IF RD-Agent executes browser/API actions based on unverified prompt content
mitigations: Require human review of imported prompts
Add a verification step before any action-taking
Limit RD-Agent to read-only runs for prompt evaluation
Log source provenance for each prompt template
requires-engineering: gate action execution on signed templates

E_compliance.rationale: RD-Agent explicitly handles financial reports, logs, execution traces, and external API keys, which creates compliance obligations around retention and residency. awesome-prompts is a public open-source prompt repository and does not itself show regulated data handling, so the compliance risk is mainly from RD-Agent’s documented data classes and outbound APIs. The mismatch is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed through RD-Agent
IF outbound API providers are outside the required residency or DPA boundary
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in RD-Agent runs
Confirm provider DPAs and residency settings
Separate public prompt repositories from regulated workloads
Minimize log retention
requires-engineering: implement policy-based routing for regulated data
